passage:
Avni, you asked why I looked so wrecked on Friday, so here's the honest version. I'm Anand. That week I'd spent Monday listening to my roommate's breakup, Tuesday calming a coursemate's panic before her viva, Wednesday on a call with a friend from home till one in the morning. On Thursday night, at ten, another friend rang. I watched the phone buzz on my desk and I didn't pick up.
Then I felt terrible. Like I'd done something wrong. I texted, "Can't talk tonight, can we speak tomorrow evening?" and then sat there with my stomach in a knot.
Later I realised I'd been saying yes to everyone for months, and that's why saying no felt like betrayal. I still don't know if I'm a bad friend. But I was tired, and that's true too.

qa.q: What time did the friend ring on Thursday night?
qa.a: The friend rang at ten.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling after letting the phone ring and texting about tomorrow?
qa.a: Anand felt guilty and anxious, as though something wrong had been done, with a knot in the stomach.

qa.q: What did Anand do that made declining kinder?
qa.a: Anand sent a text saying tonight was not possible and offered to speak the next evening, so the friend was not simply ignored.

qa.q: What might Avni think about Anand's story?
qa.a: Avni may see that the guilt came from months of saying yes to everyone, not from real wrongdoing. Avni might also feel sympathy after hearing about the week.

grounding: A student who has listened to friends all week feels selfish declining another call, and the guilt reflects long over-giving.

passage:
I'm Reena. In our hostel corridor, Hafsa is the one everybody goes to. Last Saturday I was on the bed next to her when her phone lit up with a name. She looked at it for a while, then turned it face down.
"You're not going to pick up?" I asked.
"I can't tonight." She rubbed her hands together. "It's awful, I know. She always needs someone. I said sorry to her already, twice, in a message."
She sent a third sorry. Then she sat there with her jaw tight, looking like she had stolen something.
I can't know what's in her head. Maybe she really is being selfish, or maybe it's the fifth call this week. I said, "You listened to three people yesterday. It's okay to be tired." She didn't answer, but she didn't pick up either.

qa.q: How many apology messages had Hafsa sent, counting the third one?
qa.a: She had sent three apologies by the end.

qa.q: How does Hafsa seem to feel about declining the call?
qa.a: Hafsa seems guilty and uneasy, as if she had stolen something. She rubs her hands, keeps her jaw tight and apologises repeatedly.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try instead of sending sorry after sorry?
qa.a: Hafsa could send one short message that she cannot talk tonight and when she can, then leave the phone alone. That names the limit once without over-apologising.

qa.q: What might Reena be worried about as Hafsa sits with a tight jaw?
qa.a: Reena seems unsure and concerned. Reena says it is impossible to know what is in Hafsa's head, but offers a kind reminder that listening to three people the day before is tiring.

grounding: A hostel-mate sees a peer feel guilty about declining another call after a week of listening.

passage: Mridul's phone lit up at 10:40 pm in the Mukherjee Nagar PG room. Tenzin again. It was the fifth night this week: the roommate who stole his milk, the girl who stopped replying, the landlord. Mridul had listened every time, sometimes for an hour. Tonight Mridul had a viva at nine and a headache that wouldn't quit. The phone kept buzzing. Mridul typed: "Hey, I'm wiped out tonight. Can we talk at lunch tomorrow? I promise I'll listen properly then." He hovered over send for a long time, feeling like a traitor. Then he sent it. Tenzin replied, "oh ok sure 👍" and nothing else. Mridul lay awake anyway, sure he'd been selfish. It took until the next day, at lunch, when Tenzin started with "sorry for dumping on you all week," for Mridul to breathe out.

qa.q: What time did Mridul's phone light up?
qa.a: At 10:40 pm.

qa.q: Why did Mridul feel like a traitor before sending the message?
qa.a: Mridul had listened every night that week, so declining felt selfish and guilty, even though he was exhausted and had a viva.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering a specific time to talk at lunch worked, because it protected Mridul's rest while keeping the promise of real support.

qa.q: How did Tenzin see the week of calls?
qa.a: At lunch Tenzin apologised for dumping on Mridul all week, which suggests Tenzin felt a bit guilty and did not think the no was selfish.

grounding: Shows a student who has listened to a friend all week feeling selfish for declining one more call, though the guilt came from habit, not wrongdoing.

passage:
"Your phone's buzzing again," Manoj said from the other bed.
"It's Isha," Pallavi said. "Fourth call this week."
"About the same breakup?"
"Yes. And yesterday it was Farhan's internship, and Monday it was Meenal's mum."
"You've got the anatomy test tomorrow."
"I know." Pallavi stared at the screen. "If I don't pick up, I'm a terrible friend."
"Are you? What did you do wrong?"
She opened her mouth. Closed it. "Nothing, I guess. I just always pick up."
"So maybe the guilt is just habit."
The phone stopped. Pallavi typed quickly: "Isha, I'm so sorry, exam tomorrow, can I call you after at 5?"
Isha replied with a heart and "all the best!! 💪"
Pallavi let out a long breath. "She's fine."
"Of course she is," Manoj said. "Now open your anatomy notes."

qa.q: How many times had Isha called that week?
qa.a: It was the fourth call this week.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling as she stared at the screen?
qa.a: She felt guilty and torn, believing not picking up would make her a terrible friend, even though she had an anatomy test.

qa.q: How did Manoj help Pallavi without telling her what to do?
qa.a: He asked what she had actually done wrong, so she noticed herself that the guilt came from habit, not wrongdoing.

qa.q: How did Isha react to Pallavi's message?
qa.a: Isha replied with a heart and wished her luck, so she felt supported rather than rejected.

grounding: Shows a student who feels selfish declining another friend's call after a week of listening, and realises the guilt comes from over-giving.

passage:
Last Thursday I did something small that felt enormous: I didn't take Ojas's call.
I'd spent that whole week holding people up. Monday, Ojas's fight with his dad. Tuesday, my lab partner's panic about marks. Wednesday, two hours on the stairs with a girl from my floor who'd just moved from Imphal and was homesick.
Thursday night the phone rang again and my whole body sank. I let it ring, then texted: "Can't tonight, I'm done in. Tomorrow after class?"
Then I sat there feeling like a monster. I kept rereading the text for hidden cruelty. There wasn't any.
Ojas sent back "no worries, bro." The next day he said he'd sorted most of it himself.
I think I felt guilty because saying yes is what I always do, not because saying no was wrong. I'm Pranav, by the way, and I'm still practising.

qa.q: Where had the girl on the narrator's floor moved from?
qa.a: She had just moved from Imphal.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling after sending the text?
qa.a: Pranav felt guilty, like a monster, rereading the message for cruelty even though there was none.

qa.q: What small step could Pranav keep using?
qa.a: Pranav could keep offering a clear later time, like 'tomorrow after class,' when already drained, instead of taking every call.

qa.q: How did Ojas take Pranav's text?
qa.a: Ojas replied 'no worries, bro' and sorted most of it himself, so he did not feel abandoned.

grounding: Shows a student feeling guilty for declining one call after a week of listening, and recognising the guilt as a habit of over-giving.

passage:
College counselling centre, session note, Friday.
Ramesh came in about poor sleep, but his phone buzzed four times during the hour. Each time it was Eshaan. This week Ramesh has taken late-night calls from three friends about a breakup, marks and a fight at home, most nights until two. Tonight Eshaan wants to talk again about an argument in their project group. Ramesh said, "If I don't pick up, I'm a selfish person." His hands were shaking a little. I asked when he had last said no to anyone. He could not remember. We practised one line: "I care, and I can't talk tonight. Tomorrow at lunch?" He sent it while still in the room, then sat with his eyes shut. Eshaan replied: "ok, lunch 👍". Follow-up next Friday.

qa.q: How many times did Ramesh's phone buzz during the hour?
qa.a: It buzzed four times.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he said he would be a selfish person?
qa.a: He felt guilty and anxious, his hands shaking a little, as if saying no would be a real wrong.

qa.q: Why did the practised line help?
qa.a: It kept the care and offered a clear time, so Ramesh could rest tonight without dropping his friend 👍

qa.q: How did Eshaan respond to the message, and what does it show?
qa.a: Eshaan simply agreed to lunch, which shows the no did not hurt the friendship the way Ramesh feared.

grounding: Shows a student worn out from listening to friends all week feeling guilty about declining a call, and a counsellor helping him say no kindly.
